claims.claim: Illinois passed the Juvenile Court Act in 1899, establishing the nation's first separate juvenile court in Cook County; the British doctrine of parens patriae - the state as parent - supplied the rationale for intervening in children's lives differently from adults'. The legislature passed the law on April 14, 1899, and the Cook County court opened July 3, 1899. By 1910, 32 states had juvenile courts and/or probation services; by 1925, all but two states had followed.

Juvenile court practice uses a distinct vocabulary. A delinquency petition states the allegations and asks the court to adjudicate the youth delinquent; the criminal court equivalent is that a person is convicted and sentenced. A delinquent offense is an act committed by a juvenile for which an adult could be prosecuted in criminal court. Probation was the most severe disposition ordered in 65 percent of cases in which a youth was adjudicated delinquent in 2019.

A status offense is conduct that is a violation only because of the actor's age; federal law defines a status offender as a juvenile charged with or who has committed an offense that would not be criminal if committed by an adult. State statutes commonly identify truancy, running away, and ungovernability as status offenses.

The JJDP Act's 'core requirements' are defined by statute as the requirements in paragraphs (11), (12), (13), and (15) of 34 U.S.C. 11133(a): deinstitutionalization of status offenders, no sight or sound contact with adult inmates, removal of juveniles from adult jails and lockups (subject to narrow exceptions such as a six-hour processing window and a rural 48-hour exception), and policy and practice strategies to identify and reduce racial and ethnic disparities. Paragraph (11) carries an exception for a juvenile who violates a valid court order. Paragraph (15) expressly forbids establishing or requiring numerical standards or quotas.
The JJDP Act of 1974 was reauthorized and substantially amended by the Juvenile Justice Reform Act of 2018, signed into law in December 2018 (Public Law 115-385, enacted December 21, 2018).

Kent v. United States, 383 U.S. 541, argued January 19, 1966 and decided March 21, 1966 (Fortas, J., for the Court; Stewart, J., joined by Black, Harlan, and White, JJ., dissenting), held that as a condition of a valid waiver order the juvenile was entitled to a hearing, to access by his counsel to the social records considered by the court, and to a statement of reasons for the decision - a result the Court said was required by the statute read in the context of constitutional principles relating to due process and the assistance of counsel.

In re Gault, 387 U.S. 1, argued December 6, 1966 and decided May 15, 1967 (Fortas, J., for the Court; Stewart, J., dissenting), held that in delinquency adjudications that may result in commitment, due process requires adequate written notice of the specific charges, notice of the right to counsel and to appointed counsel if indigent, the privilege against self-incrimination, and the rights of confrontation and cross-examination of sworn witnesses. The Court expressly did not rule on appellate review or a transcript. Gerald Gault was 15; his commitment could run to age 21 - a maximum of six years - while an adult convicted of the same offense faced a fine of $5 to $50 or up to two months in jail.

In re Winship, 397 U.S. 358 (1970), held that proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the charged offense is required in a juvenile delinquency adjudication, rejecting the argument that a civil label removes the need for criminal due process safeguards. The case arose from a 12-year-old adjudicated delinquent under a New York preponderance standard.

McKeiver v. Pennsylvania, 403 U.S. 528, decided June 21, 1971, held that trial by jury is not constitutionally required in the adjudicative phase of a state juvenile court delinquency proceeding. Justice Blackmun announced the judgment in an opinion joined by Burger, C.J., and Stewart and White, JJ.; White, Brennan, and Harlan, JJ., wrote separately; Douglas, J., dissented, joined by Black and Marshall, JJ. The plurality said states remain free to install a jury system or to let a judge use an advisory jury.

Breed v. Jones, 421 U.S. 519, decided May 27, 1975 in a unanimous opinion by Chief Justice Burger, held that prosecuting a youth as an adult after a juvenile court adjudicatory finding that he violated a criminal statute violates the Double Jeopardy Clause; jeopardy attached when the juvenile court, as trier of fact, began to hear evidence.

Transfer provisions fall into three general categories. As of 2019, judicial waiver by a juvenile court judge was available in 47 states, statutory exclusion of certain cases from juvenile court jurisdiction existed in 27 states, and prosecutorial discretion (concurrent jurisdiction, also called direct file) existed in 14 states. Judicial waiver goes by other names in some states, including certification, remand, and bind over. In 35 states, statutes require that a youth once tried as an adult be prosecuted in criminal court for subsequent offenses.

Nothing compels a state to draw the juvenile/adult line at 18. In 8 states during 2019, the upper age of juvenile court jurisdiction was 15 or 16. As of the end of the 2019 legislative session, statutes in 34 states extended juvenile court jurisdiction in delinquency cases to the 21st birthday for disposition purposes.

Roper v. Simmons, 543 U.S. 551, decided March 1, 2005 (Kennedy, J., for a five-Justice majority; O'Connor, J., and Scalia, J., joined by Rehnquist, C.J., and Thomas, J., dissenting), held that the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments forbid imposing the death penalty on offenders who were under 18 when their crimes were committed. The Court identified three general differences between juveniles and adults: a lack of maturity and an underdeveloped sense of responsibility; greater vulnerability to negative influences and outside pressures including peer pressure; and a character that is not as well formed.

Graham v. Florida, 560 U.S. 48, decided May 17, 2010 (Kennedy, J., for the Court), held that the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause does not permit a juvenile offender to be sentenced to life without parole for a nonhomicide crime. A state need not guarantee eventual freedom, but must give such defendants some meaningful opportunity to obtain release based on demonstrated maturity and rehabilitation.

Miller v. Alabama, 567 U.S. 460, decided June 25, 2012 (Kagan, J., for a five-Justice majority), held that the Eighth Amendment forbids a sentencing scheme that mandates life without parole for juvenile homicide offenders. The Court expressly declined to reach the argument for a categorical bar, and said appropriate occasions for the sentence would be 'uncommon'. Miller is therefore a rule about mandatory sentencing, not an outright prohibition.

Montgomery v. Louisiana, 577 U.S. 190, decided January 25, 2016 (Kennedy, J., for the Court; Scalia, J., joined by Thomas and Alito, JJ., and Thomas, J., dissenting), held that Miller announced a substantive rule of constitutional law and therefore applies retroactively in cases on state collateral review; a state may remedy a Miller violation by extending parole eligibility rather than resentencing.

Jones v. Mississippi, No. 18-1259, decided April 22, 2021 (Kavanaugh, J., for the Court, joined by Roberts, C.J., and Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett, JJ.; Thomas, J., concurring in the judgment; Sotomayor, J., dissenting, joined by Breyer and Kagan, JJ.), held that Miller and Montgomery do not require a sentencer to make a separate factual finding of permanent incorrigibility, or an on-the-record sentencing explanation implying such a finding, before imposing life without parole on a defendant who committed a homicide under 18. A discretionary sentencing system is both constitutionally necessary and constitutionally sufficient. The Court stated that its decision does not disturb Miller's or Montgomery's holdings.

The developmental research the Court cited does not say adolescents are globally immature. In the MacArthur Juvenile Capacity Study of 935 participants aged 10 to 30, general cognitive abilities were essentially indistinguishable from adults' by about age 16, while psychosocial maturity at 18 remained significantly below that of people in their mid-twenties; the authors distinguish unhurried, logical decisions from situations involving emotional arousal, peer coercion, or impulsivity.

The one-day count of youth in residential placement held for an offense fell 72 percent between 1997 and 2023. On the October 25, 2023 census date, 89 percent of residents in juvenile residential placement facilities were held for an offense, 81 percent of youth were in public facilities, and 56 percent of those were in local facilities. OJJDP notes the COVID-19 pandemic may have affected the 2020-2022 collections. In 2019, youth were detained at some point between referral and disposition in 26 percent of juvenile court delinquency cases.

Using the October 25, 2023 Census of Juveniles in Residential Placement, national placement rates for youth of color other than Asian/Pacific Islander youth exceeded the rate for white youth: the rate for Black youth was more than 5 times the white rate, the rate for American Indian youth nearly 4 times, and the rate for Hispanic youth 1.3 times. In all but 9 states the Black placement rate exceeded the rate for other race and ethnicity groups. These are measured rates; the data do not by themselves establish a cause.

CrimeSolutions rates the practice 'Juvenile Awareness Programs (Scared Straight)' Ineffective. Its meta-analytic evidence found participants had higher reoffending rates than nonparticipants: Aos and colleagues (2001) reported a small negative effect size across eight studies, and Petrosino, Petrosino, and Buehler (2004) found the programs increased the odds of offending (odds ratio 1.47). The profile was posted September 10, 2013 and carries a notice that the page is no longer being updated.

By contrast, CrimeSolutions rates Functional Family Therapy (FFT), a family-based program for youth ages 11 to 18 who are justice-involved or at risk, Effective, based on evidence including at least one high-quality randomized controlled trial; participants showed a statistically significant reduction in general recidivism and risky behavior, with no differences on felony recidivism or caregiver strengths and needs. The profile was posted June 14, 2011 and carries a notice that the page is no longer being updated.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Miller v. Alabama banned life without parole for juveniles
positions: A common secondary framing treats Miller as abolishing juvenile life without parole outright.
Miller's own text forbids only a mandatory scheme, expressly declines to reach a categorical bar, and predicts the sentence will be 'uncommon'.
Montgomery called Miller substantive because it rendered the penalty unconstitutional for a class - juveniles whose crimes reflect transient immaturity - which reads Miller more broadly.
Jones v. Mississippi held that no separate finding of permanent incorrigibility and no on-the-record explanation is required, and that a discretionary system is constitutionally sufficient.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the sequence in the order the Court decided it and quotes each holding at its own scope: Miller bars mandatory imposition, Montgomery makes that retroactive, and Jones materially narrows how much process Miller and Montgomery demand at sentencing. The lesson does not describe juvenile life without parole as abolished by the Eighth Amendment, because no opinion so holds.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What explains racial and ethnic disparities in juvenile placement
positions: The disparities are measured facts in OJJDP's census data.

Competing explanations - differential offending, differential system contact and decision-making, and differences in community and family resources - are contested in the research literature and not resolved by the census.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the measured placement rates and their date, names the JJDP Act requirement that states analyze data at decision points, and states plainly that the census establishes the pattern and not its cause.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Counts of states using each transfer mechanism
positions: The 2022 National Report gives 2019 counts (47 judicial waiver, 27 statutory exclusion, 14 prosecutorial discretion).
The Statistical Briefing Book hosts updated state-by-state versions through the 2023 data year.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the dated 2019 figures from the National Report, labels them as of 2019, and points readers to the Statistical Briefing Book for current state-by-state detail. The interactive Briefing Book tables render through a Tableau service and were read as the underlying CSV exports.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's framing of juvenile justice as a generic 'foundational concept' that students use to 'organize information' - it named no institution, no statute, and no case, and nothing in the research supports treating the topic that way.
The draft's claim that the lesson's purpose is to 'apply juvenile justice to a simple scenario' with no jurisdictional content.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') are not juvenile justice terms and were not supportable as such.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft, which contained no verifiable subject-matter content.

Stated Miller v. Alabama at its actual scope (mandatory schemes) rather than as a categorical ban, and placed Jones v. Mississippi after Montgomery as the decision that limited what Miller and Montgomery require at sentencing.
Stated McKeiver's holding as no constitutional right to a jury in the adjudicative phase, noting it was a plurality announcement and that states may provide juries anyway.
Recorded Kent as a decision resting on the District of Columbia statute read in light of due process and right-to-counsel principles, rather than as a freestanding constitutional holding.
Dated every quantitative figure and named the collection (CJRP census date October 25, 2023; National Report 2019 data year).
rightsIssues: U.S. Supreme Court opinions and the United States Code are edicts of government and carry no copyright; the govinfo United States Reports PDFs and the uscode.house.gov text were read directly.

Jones v. Mississippi is not yet available in a govinfo United States Reports volume, so the Court's own slip opinion is the registered URL. The lesson cites the case by docket number and decision date rather than an unverified U.S. Reports page.
OJJDP and CrimeSolutions pages state no reuse license, so they are recorded REFERENCE_ONLY; their facts are used, none of their prose.
The Steinberg et al. (2009) article is copyrighted by the American Psychological Association and is used REFERENCE_ONLY for its findings.
No source prose was reproduced beyond short doctrinal phrases from public-domain opinions and statutory text.
